newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam's PM calls for mass labour mobilisation.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam's PM calls for mass labour mobilisation.

text.p: Vietnam's Prime Minister Vo Van Kiet, considered a leading proponent of economic reforms, called on Tuesday for a revival of 1950s-style labour policies involving millions of people in vast construction projects.

Kiet, 74, said in an interview with the official Vietnam News Agency (VNA) that mass mobilisation of the country's workforce was needed in order to modernise Vietnam's crumbling national infrastructure.

"A far-reaching movement must be launched to carry on the great mettle of the nation with which we will march towards a new peak -- to rid the country of poverty and take it along the road of industrialisation and modernisation," he said, adding:
"This is a natural course of things, not just some novel notion."

VNA said Kiet recalled a series of historical precedents for the policy including the involvement of millions of people in projects such as the construction in the late 1950s of an irrigation system near Hanoi, the Cu Chi infiltration tunnels near Saigon, and the Ho Chi Minh trail.

Both the Cu Chi tunnels -- preserved today as a Viet Cong theme park -- and the Ho Chi Minh trail, used to ferry Hanoi's ordnance and troops to and from the U.S.-backed South, are viewed as symbols of wartime resilience and ingenuity.

The VNA interview provided few details, but according to recent prime ministerial proposals, "all citizens within working age, barring those with exemptions" will be required to participate in an expanded compulsory labour programme.

Under the plan people between the ages of 18 and 45 will pay to be excluded or work without salary on infrastructure projects for a fixed number of days each year, supplementing a force made up of young men who fail to meet the requirements for military national service.

The move -- envisaging construction of projects including a new north-south expressway -- has drawn fire from both domestic and foreign economists, with some likening it to the disastrous labour mobilisation policies of China's Mao Zedong.
But in apparent recognition of such criticism, Kiet said prospective labourers would be assessed to ensure that intellectuals and professionals were not being drafted away from more useful tasks.
"If workers from specialist professions have to give up work to do simple labour, then it will be a waste," he said.
Hanoi-based analysts appeared confused by Kiet's remarks on Tuesday and said they had not been informed of any change in policy by government officials.

Vietnam has operated a system of small-scale self-help labour projects for many years, but they said the absence of discussion of the matter with international agencies indicated Kiet's proposals might be aimed primarily at addressing internal politics.

"Nobody has any idea why he would come out and say something like this just before Tet (the lunar new year)," one said. "He said something like this during the National Assembly session last year, but this time it's a bit more specific."

Hanoi introduced market-oriented Doi Moi (renovation) policies in 1986 in place of a failed Soviet-style system. Vo Van Kiet, a member of the leadership triumvirate, is considered a leading champion of those reforms.
